title: Play in the style of Jimi Hendrix
goal: Learn Hendrix the way he did: R&B rhythm and thumb-over chords first, then the embellishments, lead voice and fuzz tone.

steps.title: Where Hendrix came from, and how to tune like him
steps.description:
[Before you start]
This roadmap assumes an intermediate player: barre chords, the minor pentatonic in at least two positions, a whole-step bend that lands in tune, and enough rhythm to hold a 12-bar blues. A guitar with a tremolo arm helps in one phase but is not required. By the end you will play his rhythm style (thumb chords, partial shapes, sliding sixths, muted comping), the embellishment method behind Little Wing, the 7#9 chord riffs, his lead vocabulary, a tone close to his on your own gear, seven songs, and a recorded set of your own.

[What it is]
Two practical facts to set up before anything else. First, the schooling: before the Experience, Hendrix spent years on the chitlin' circuit as a backing guitarist, joining the Isley Brothers' band in 1964 and touring with Little Richard's Upsetters from late that year, and also backing Wilson Pickett, Sam Cooke, Ike and Tina Turner, Jackie Wilson and King Curtis. Second, the tuning: his records are almost all a half step down, so the sixth string is E flat and everything sits a semitone below standard.

[Why it matters]
The R&B years are the reason his rhythm playing is the deepest part of his style, and they are why this roadmap starts with chords rather than with solos. The tuning matters just as practically: if you play along with the records in standard tuning nothing lines up, and the slacker strings are part of why his bends go as far as they do. He used heavy strings by modern standards, reported by his technician Roger Mayer as .010 to .038, so the lower tension bought back the bendability.

[How to practice]
Tune the whole guitar down a half step and leave it there for this roadmap; check it with a tuner set to E flat or drop each string by one semitone against a reference. Then play a slow 12-bar in E (which now sounds in E flat) in Chord Practice — Pick Your Chords, using E7, A7 and B7, thinking of yourself as the guitarist behind a singer: no fills over the vocal, everything in the gaps. Listen to one track per session from the list: Curtis Mayfield and the Impressions, Booker T. and the MGs for Steve Cropper, then Muddy Waters, B.B. King and Howlin' Wolf, then Are You Experienced.
steps.successCriteria: Your guitar is tuned a half step down and stays there, you can play a 12-bar in E with E7, A7 and B7 leaving space for a vocal, and you can name four R&B or blues acts he played with or learned from and say what each contributed.

lessons.title: Rhythm Chops; Hendrix-isms, Soul Riffs & Blues Double Stops to level up your Chords! John Mayer vibe

steps.title: Thumb over the neck
steps.description:
[What it is]
Wrapping the fretting-hand thumb over the top of the neck to fret the root on the sixth string, instead of barring with the first finger. The thumb also mutes the fifth string, and the first, second, third and fourth fingers are then free to hold the rest of the chord and to move.

[Why it matters]
This single change is what makes the rest of his rhythm style possible. MusicRadar puts it plainly: wrapping the thumb round the neck to fret the sixth string means "chord embellishments fell neatly under his fingers". A barre chord uses all four fingers to hold a sound; a thumb chord uses two or three and keeps the little finger free to add the notes that turn a chord into a part.

[How to practice]
Push the neck away from you slightly and let the wrist drop so the thumb can reach over. Start with an E-shape at the fifth fret: thumb on the fifth fret of the sixth string, and only the fourth, third and second strings fretted underneath. Check the fifth string is silenced by the thumb's underside. Play Muting — Inside a D Chord, which trains exactly this kind of selective silencing. Then move the grip through A, B and C along the sixth string, and play a 12-bar with thumb-fretted chords only, keeping the little finger hovering free the whole time.
steps.successCriteria: You can hold thumb-fretted major and minor shapes at four positions with the root clean and the fifth string silent, change between them in a 12-bar without the thumb slipping, and keep the little finger free and hovering throughout.

lessons.title: Hendrix Style: How to Use Your Thumb to Play Chord Bass Notes on Guitar
Jimi Hendrix Thumb Chords - Rhythm Guitar Lesson
Thumb Barre Chords - How and Why - Jimi Hendrix, John Frusciante, John Mayer Rhythm Guitar Tutorial
The Hendrix Thumb Trick

steps.title: Partial shapes: two or three notes of a chord
steps.description:
[What it is]
Playing only part of a chord: a one-finger barre across three adjacent strings, a pair of notes from the top of a shape, or an inversion that puts the third rather than the root in the bass. The rest of the chord is either muted or simply left out.

[Why it matters]
MusicRadar calls the one-finger three-string barre "a key part of Jimi's rhythm style" and describes his method as "playing only two or three notes from each shape". Partial chords cut through a trio mix where a full six-string chord turns to mud, they leave the bass player room, and they move faster because the hand barely changes. They are also what the embellishment work in the next phase hangs on: you cannot decorate a chord if all four fingers are holding it.

[How to practice]
Take a thumb-fretted E-shape and remove notes one at a time until only three strings sound, then two; play the progression with each reduction and hear what survives. Learn the one-finger barre on the third, second and first strings as both a major and a minor shape and move it through a progression. Play Chords — Smooth Changes on a fixed three-string set so the hand learns to stay put. Then play a I to IV change using only inversions, keeping the top note as close as possible.
steps.successCriteria: You can play a I–IV–V progression three ways — full thumb chords, three-string partials and two-note fragments — with every unwanted string silent, and you can put the third in the bass of any major or minor chord you use.

lessons.title: 3 Essential Chord Shapes for Guitar - Chord Inversions Guitar Lesson - EP199

steps.title: Sliding sixths and soul double stops
steps.description:
[What it is]
Two notes a sixth apart on non-adjacent strings, moved through a scale so the pair slides up and down the neck, plus the double stops in fourths and thirds that fill the same role. The string between the two fretted notes is muted, so the shape can be strummed rather than picked.

[Why it matters]
This is the soul vocabulary Hendrix took from Curtis Mayfield and Steve Cropper, and he said so: of the 1963 tour with the Impressions he said Mayfield "probably influenced me more than anyone I'd ever played with up to that time, that sweet sound of his". Guitar World's analysis identifies his most common double stop as a perfect fourth moving to a minor third and back, which is the shape under most of his rhythm fills. Sixths are how a single guitar sounds like a horn section.

[How to practice]
Play Note Hunt — Intervals set to sixths until you find one instantly from any root. Then harmonise a major scale in sixths on the fourth and second strings and on the third and first, up and down the neck at 60 BPM, muting the string in between with the underside of the fretting finger. Then the fourth-to-minor-third move: find it inside an E7 shape and play it as a repeated fill over a groove. Finish by putting sixths into the gaps of the 12-bar from the first step.
steps.successCriteria: You can play a major scale in sixths on two string pairs up and down the neck at 80 BPM with the middle string silent, play the fourth-to-minor-third double stop as a fill over an E7 groove, and place both inside the gaps of a 12-bar without covering the vocal line.

steps.title: Left-hand muting and the percussive strum
steps.description:
[What it is]
Relaxing the fretting fingers so the strings are damped but still touched, then strumming: the result is rhythm without pitch. Alternated with sounded chords it makes the guitar part percussive, and it lets the strumming hand keep moving while only chosen beats have harmony.

[Why it matters]
Dale Turner's analysis of his rhythm playing lists muting as one of the pillars, used to "dampen the strings" so only chosen notes ring, producing the percussive, funk-oriented effect. In a trio with no second guitar, the muted strum is what keeps the groove alive between chord hits. It is also the only way partial chords stay clean: the strings you are not using have to be dead, not quiet.

[How to practice]
Play Muting — Both Hands to set up the two-hand system. Then hold a thumb chord and alternate one sounded strum with three muted ones for two minutes at 80 BPM, checking that the muted strums have no pitch at all. Move the sounded strum to different beats. Then play the 12-bar with the chord sounding only on beats one and three, everything else muted, and listen for whether the part still grooves.
steps.successCriteria: A two-minute recording of alternating sounded and muted strums at 85 BPM has no pitch audible in the muted strums, no unwanted ring under the partials, and a groove a listener can follow when only beats one and three sound.

lessons.title: Guitar String Muting Techniques - How To Play Guitar - Stage 3 Guitar Lesson [IM-134]
Rhythm Guitar Lesson Using String Muting Techniques

steps.title: Sixteenth-note R&B comping
steps.description:
[What it is]
The strumming hand moving in continuous sixteenths while the fretting hand decides which of them ring: partial chords on some, muted scratches on the rest, sixths as fills at the ends of phrases. The result is the tight, funk-leaning rhythm part behind a vocal.

[Why it matters]
This is the job he was actually hired for on the circuit, and it is the engine of "Crosstown Traffic", "Can You See Me" and the Band of Gypsys material. It puts the four previous steps together: thumb chords, partials, sixths and muting are individually easy and simultaneously hard. A guitarist who can do this can play behind a singer in any soul or funk band.

[How to practice]
Play Strumming — Funk 16ths at 70 to 90 BPM for the hand. Then apply it to a two-chord vamp with thumb chords: two ringing stabs per bar, scratches on everything else, and a sixths fill in the last beat of every other bar. Record over a drum loop at 95 BPM and check that the groove, not the guitar, is what you notice. Then play the same part while singing or humming a melody, to prove it leaves room.
steps.successCriteria: Over a drum loop at 90–100 BPM you can comp a two-chord R&B vamp for three minutes with a constant sixteenth-note hand, only the chosen stabs ringing, scratches unpitched, and a sixths fill every other bar — while humming a melody over the top without the part getting in its way.

lessons.title: Comping Rhythms - 10 Examples You Need To Know
How to create GROOVE in strumming - The 2 Essential Techniques

steps.title: Hammer-ons and pull-offs around a chord shape
steps.description:
[What it is]
Holding a chord with the thumb and two fingers and using the free fingers to hammer on and pull off notes above it, so a melody appears on top of a sustained chord without the chord stopping. The chord does not change; the decoration moves.

[Why it matters]
This is the Hendrix rhythm signature and the technique behind "Little Wing", "Castles Made of Sand", "The Wind Cries Mary" and "Bold as Love". Premier Guitar describes the method as hammer-ons and pull-offs "creating melodies that sit atop sustained chord tones". It is also why the thumb work of the previous phase matters: the fingers can only decorate if they are not holding the chord.

[How to practice]
Take a thumb-fretted G at the third fret. Hold the bass and the two lowest fretted notes; with the little finger hammer the note two frets above the top chord tone and pull off, in time, on beats two and four. Keep the chord sounding underneath. Play Legato — Hammer-on Pentatonic slowly to get the hammer as loud as the picked note. Move the same decoration to C and D, then to minor shapes. Then do it over a slow 6/8 groove so the decorations land musically rather than mechanically.
steps.successCriteria: Over a slow groove you can hold a thumb-fretted chord and add hammer-on and pull-off decorations on beats two and four for two minutes, with the chord still ringing underneath and the hammered notes as loud as the picked ones, on three different shapes.

steps.title: Choosing the notes: sus, add and the next scale degree
steps.description:
[What it is]
Deciding which note to decorate with. The default is the next scale degree above or below a chord tone, which turns a major chord into a sus4 or add9 on the way past. The choice can come from the key of the whole song or from the key of the chord you are on at that moment.

[Why it matters]
"Little Wing" is the textbook case: in E minor, Hendrix takes some fills from the key itself and some from the chord of the moment, adding a C sharp in the B minor bar and an F natural in the second A minor bar. Premier Guitar summarises the general rule as ornamenting with "the next scale degree". Knowing which pool to draw from is the difference between decoration that sounds composed and decoration that sounds like a wrong note.

[How to practice]
Use Chords — Degree Hunt (Triads) until you can find the root, third and fifth of any chord instantly; the decorations sit next to those. Then take one chord and add, one at a time, the second, the fourth and the sixth above it, listening to each as a sus or add colour. Then take a four-chord progression and write two versions of the same fill: one using only notes from the key, one using a note that belongs only to the chord you are on. Play both and decide which you prefer where.
steps.successCriteria: For any chord in a four-chord progression you can name and play the sus4, the add9 and the sixth above it, and you can play two different fills over the same bar, one diatonic to the key and one taken from the chord of the moment, and say which is which.

steps.title: Double-stop embellishments
steps.description:
[What it is]
Decorating with two notes instead of one: a higher note held while a hammer-on happens on the string below it, a pair of notes slid into place from a fret below, or a double stop bent slightly so both notes move together.

[Why it matters]
Guitar World's analysis of his rhythm playing describes exactly this shape: a higher note rings throughout while the hammered embellishment happens on the lower string, with the extra notes falling near the basic chord shape and the thumb holding any sixth-string root. Two notes fill more of the space than one, which is what a trio guitarist needs, and the moving inner voice is what makes the part sound like more than one guitar.

[How to practice]
Play Phrasing — Two Notes Per Bar over a slow backing so you are forced to make two notes carry a bar. Then, inside a thumb-fretted chord, hold the top note with the little finger and hammer the note below it with the ring finger, keeping both sounding. Slide the pair up two frets and back. Put the figure on the last two beats of every bar of a two-chord vamp and record a minute of it.
steps.successCriteria: Inside a held chord you can keep a top note ringing while hammering the note below it, slide the resulting pair two frets and back cleanly, and place the figure at the same point in every bar of a two-chord vamp for a minute without the chord dropping out.

lessons.title: The magic of DOUBLE STOPS - guitar lesson / tutorial
The Double Stop: A Blues Rhythm / Lead Guitar Lesson

steps.title: Bass lines and moving inner voices under the chords
steps.description:
[What it is]
The thumb moving while the fingers hold: a bass note walking from the root to the third or the fifth under a held shape, or the chord staying put while the bass steps down chromatically. Also the reverse, an inner voice moving while root and melody stay fixed.

[Why it matters]
Once the thumb is fretting, it can play a line rather than a single root, which is how one guitar covers both the bass movement and the harmony in a song like "Castles Made of Sand". Premier Guitar notes his habit of inverting chords to put the third in the bass, which is this idea applied at the chord level. A moving bass also makes a static progression sound like it is going somewhere.

[How to practice]
Play Hybrid Picking — Bass + Chords to separate the low voice from the upper ones. Then hold a thumb-fretted G and move the thumb from the third fret to the second and back while the fingers keep the shape, listening to the chord change quality. Do the same walking from the root down to the fifth below. Then take a four-bar progression and write a bass line that connects each chord to the next by step.
steps.successCriteria: You can hold a chord shape and move the thumb through at least three bass notes under it without the upper voices moving, and play a four-bar progression whose bass line connects every chord to the next by step.

lessons.title: Cool Bass Technique for Chords, Palm Muting, and Great Tone! - Thumb and Fingers Plucking

steps.title: Sliding voicings and chromatic approach chords
steps.description:
[What it is]
Arriving at a chord from a fret below or above by sliding the whole shape into place, and passing through chords that do not belong to the key on the way between two that do. The shape does not change; only its position does.

[Why it matters]
Sliding into a chord gives the change a push that a clean arrival does not, and it is everywhere in his rhythm parts, especially on partial shapes where the slide is easy. Chromatic approach chords come from the same R&B vocabulary as the sixths: they are how a soul guitarist connects two chords a whole step apart. Both tricks also hide a slow hand, because the slide covers the moment of the change.

[How to practice]
Play Chords — Least Finger Motion so the hand learns to keep common tones. Then take a three-string partial and slide into every chord of a progression from one fret below, landing exactly on the beat. Then insert a passing chord a semitone below the target on the last eighth note of the bar. Record and check the slides sound intentional rather than late.
steps.successCriteria: You can slide into every chord of a four-chord progression from a fret below and land on the beat, add a chromatic passing chord on the last eighth of a bar, and a recording shows the slides as deliberate rather than late arrivals.

lessons.title: Embellish Your Rhythms + Chords Like Hendrix

steps.title: The Hendrix chord: 7#9
steps.description:
[What it is]
The dominant seventh with a sharpened ninth, known as the Hendrix chord because of what he did with it. In E: the open sixth string as the root, the middle finger at the seventh fret of the fifth string, the index at the sixth fret of the fourth string for the major third, the ring finger at the seventh fret of the third string for the flat seventh, and the little finger at the eighth fret of the second string for the sharp ninth.

[Why it matters]
The chord contains both the major third and, spelled as a sharp ninth, the minor third, which is the sound of the blues compressed into one grip, and it is why "Purple Haze" sounds the way it does. MusicRadar calls it his most recognisable signature chord, "hard, edgy sounding"; Dale Turner points at the tension it creates against the minor third and at its use in "Spanish Castle Magic". It is also the gateway to the rest of dominant harmony in the next step.

[How to practice]
Learn the E shape first and check every note individually; the sharp ninth is the one people mute by accident. Then move the shape up as a rootless grip on the fifth, fourth, third and second strings so it works in any key. Use Chords — Degree Hunt (Tensions) to find ninths, elevenths and thirteenths around a chord, because the sharp ninth is only the first of these colours. Then play a slow 12-bar in E using 7#9 on every chord.
steps.successCriteria: You can play the E7#9 with every note sounding, including the sharp ninth, move the rootless grip to three other keys, and play a 12-bar in E using 7#9 voicings on all three chords without the shape buzzing.

lessons.title: E7#9 Chord Guitar Lesson | The HENDRIX CHORD EXPLAINED
Dominant Jazz Chord Extensions - How to Play Jazz Guitar Lesson [JA-023]

steps.title: Dominant sevenths and ninths everywhere
steps.description:
[What it is]
The rest of the dominant family: the plain seventh as a full shape and as a three-note partial, the ninth chord that gives soul and funk its shimmer, and the thirteenth. All of them moveable, most of them played as partials with the root implied rather than stated.

[Why it matters]
Hendrix's harmony is dominant almost everywhere, which is what keeps his music sounding like the blues even at its most psychedelic. The ninth chord in particular is the R&B sound from the first phase. Knowing these as small moveable grips rather than as barre chords is what lets you use them inside a groove, and knowing which two notes define them (the third and the seventh) is what lets you drop everything else.

[How to practice]
Play Chords — Guide Tones so you can find the third and seventh of any dominant chord instantly, then play a 12-bar using only those two notes. Add the ninth to each. Then play the same 12-bar with a different voicing family each chorus: full sevenths, then three-string partials, then ninths, then 7#9. Keep the rhythm identical so the only thing changing is the harmony colour.
steps.successCriteria: You can play a 12-bar in E four times through with a different dominant voicing family each chorus (full sevenths, three-string partials, ninths, 7#9), keeping the rhythm identical, and can state the third and seventh of any dominant chord on request.

lessons.title: Dominant Jazz Chord Extensions - How to Play Jazz Guitar Lesson [JA-023]

steps.title: Chord riffs: riffing off a shape
steps.description:
[What it is]
Building a riff out of a chord grip rather than out of a scale: the shape is held, and single notes, double stops and stabs are drawn from around it, with the whole thing cut short by muting. "Foxey Lady" and "Purple Haze" are built this way, and so is most of what he wrote.

[Why it matters]
It is the difference between a guitarist who plays chords and one who plays parts. Because the hand stays in one shape, the riff can be dense without being difficult, and because the notes come from the chord, everything fits. Dale Turner's account of his funk figures lists exactly these ingredients: open-string and thumb voicings, double stops and chord partials. The stabs also need the muting from phase one: a chord riff that rings on is a mess.

[How to practice]
Play Strumming — Rock Accents for the attack. Then take one thumb-fretted E7#9 and build a four-bar riff using only the notes under your fingers plus the open sixth string, cutting every hit short. Vary which beat the chord lands on. Then move the same riff to a second shape in another key without changing its rhythm.
steps.successCriteria: You can play a four-bar riff of your own built entirely from one chord shape plus open strings, with every hit cut short and no ring-on, and move the same riff to another shape and key with its rhythm intact.

lessons.title: How To Play Rhythm Guitar - Using Hendrix Style Riffs - In Common Chord Progressions - Guitar Lesson
3 Hendrix Chord Tricks Every Guitarist Should Know

steps.title: Syncopation and the push
steps.description:
[What it is]
Placing chord hits and riff notes between the beats rather than on them, and changing chord half a beat early so the new harmony arrives ahead of the bar line. Counting continues on the beat while the part plays around it.

[Why it matters]
Dale Turner describes his single-note riffs as carrying "tricky syncopations articulated with muting, slurs, trills and bends", naming "If 6 Was 9", "Voodoo Child" and "Gypsy Eyes". Syncopation is what makes his rhythm parts feel like they are pulling the band forward rather than following it. It only works if the underlying pulse is solid, which is why the muting and comping work came first.

[How to practice]
Play Rhythm Training — Medium for placement of eighths and rests. Then take the chord riff you wrote and move its main hit half a beat earlier, keeping your foot on the beat; play both versions back to back and hear the difference. Then push a chord change to the last eighth of the bar and let it ring over the bar line. Count aloud throughout.
steps.successCriteria: You can play your chord riff in an on-the-beat and a syncopated version on request with the foot steady, push a chord change to the last eighth of the bar and hold it over the bar line, and count aloud through both.

lessons.title: Syncopation Explained for Guitar Players

steps.title: Triplet feel, shuffle and the slow blues
steps.description:
[What it is]
Dividing the beat in three: the shuffle that drives "Red House" and most of his blues playing, the 12/8 feel of a slow blues, and triplet figures inside otherwise straight parts. The upstroke lands late, on the third of three rather than halfway.

[Why it matters]
His blues playing is where the R&B training and the lead voice meet, and it is all in triplet time. A slow blues in 12/8 is also the most exposed rhythmic setting there is: every note's placement is audible. Getting the feel right is what separates a convincing "Red House" from a correct one.

[How to practice]
Play Timing — Triplets at 60 BPM counting "one trip-let" on each beat. Then play a 12-bar shuffle in E with thumb chords, accenting the first and third of each triplet. Then slow to a 12/8 blues at about 50 BPM and play a sparse comp with fills in the gaps. Record and compare with the studio "Red House".
steps.successCriteria: You can play a 12-bar shuffle in E with thumb chords at 90 BPM with the upstroke landing on the third triplet, and a 12/8 slow blues comp at around 50 BPM with fills in the gaps that do not rush.

lessons.title: RIFF and GROOVE HARDER with TRIPLETS!

steps.title: Bends: to pitch, past it, and back down
steps.description:
[What it is]
Whole-step and half-step bends that land exactly on a target pitch, supported by the fingers behind the bending finger and driven by wrist rotation; the pre-bend, where the string is bent silently and then struck so the pitch falls; and the slow release that brings a bent note back down in time.

[Why it matters]
Bending is the most exposed thing a lead guitarist does, and with the guitar tuned down a half step and strung with the gauges he used, the bends go further than most players expect. His phrases resolve through bends rather than through picked notes, which is why a bend that lands flat ruins a line that was otherwise fine. The pre-bend and release is the falling cry that ends many of his phrases.

[How to practice]
Play Bending — Match the Reference: sound the target, bend into it over a half note, hold, release slowly. Do whole steps on the third and second strings first, then half steps. Then pre-bends: bend silently to the target, pick, release over two beats, landing in tune. Then combine: bend up, hold with vibrato, release. Record ten of each and count how many land.
steps.successCriteria: Against a reference, nine of ten whole-step and half-step bends land in tune and hold steady, your pre-bend and release lands on the target on the way down, and you can bend, hold with vibrato and release inside one phrase.

lessons.title: Guitar Bending 101: How to Get Better at String Bends

steps.title: Vibrato: hand, and bar
steps.description:
[What it is]
Two ways of moving a held note. Finger vibrato from wrist rotation, at a width and speed you choose and with a stable pitch centre. And bar vibrato, using the tremolo arm for a shallow shimmer, a scoop into a note, or a full dive.

[Why it matters]
He used both, often on the same note, and the bar is part of why his sustained notes sound unlike anyone before him. Wikipedia credits him with pioneering the guitar as an electronic sound source; the tremolo arm is the mechanical half of that. Practically, vibrato is what keeps a long note alive under fuzz, where a straight note just sits there.

[How to practice]
Play Vibrato — Speed & Width, choosing width and speed deliberately rather than defaulting. Then hold a note plain for a beat and start a slow wide vibrato for three, keeping the pitch centre from creeping up. Then the bar: rest the hand on it and add a shallow shimmer to a held chord; scoop into a note from below; take a controlled dive and return to pitch, checking tuning afterwards. Alternate hand and bar vibrato on the same note.
steps.successCriteria: You can produce finger vibrato at two widths and two speeds on request with a stable pitch centre, add a shallow bar shimmer to a held chord, scoop into a note from below, and return from a dive with the guitar still in tune.

steps.title: Double-stop bends and unison bends
steps.description:
[What it is]
Bending one note of a two-note pair while the other stays fixed, so the interval between them changes; and the unison bend, where the lower note is bent up to match the pitch of the higher one until the two beat together and then lock.

[Why it matters]
This is the loud, aggressive end of his lead vocabulary and the reason a single line can sound like two guitars. The unison bend in particular is a blues-rock signature that needs precise pitch matching: too little and it sounds sour, too much and it sounds wrong in the other direction. It also builds directly on the double-stop work from the R&B phase, applied to lead instead of rhythm.

[How to practice]
Play Bending — Unison Bends, which trains the pitch match directly: hold the higher note, bend the lower one until the beating between them stops. Then the moving double stop: hold the top note and bend the lower one a half step, so a third becomes a fourth. Then a whole step. Work on the second and third strings, then the third and fourth. Put one into a pentatonic lick.
steps.successCriteria: Your unison bends lock with no audible beating on two string pairs, you can bend the lower note of a double stop a half and a whole step while the top note stays fixed and in tune, and you can place one of each inside a pentatonic lick.

steps.title: Octaves as a melodic voice
steps.description:
[What it is]
Playing a melody in octaves: the root on a lower string and its octave two strings up, the string in between muted by the underside of the first finger, the pair moved along the neck as a single shape. Struck with the pick or with the thumb, and often let to ring.

[Why it matters]
Octaves are how a single guitar states a theme with authority, and "Third Stone from the Sun" is the obvious case. Because the shape is fixed, an octave melody can move anywhere on the neck without thinking about position, and because the muting is built into the grip, it works under any amount of gain. It is also the cleanest way to practise the muting discipline from phase one in a lead context.

[How to practice]
Play String Skipping — Pentatonic for the crossing accuracy. Then form the octave shape on the sixth and fourth strings and move it up the neck one fret at a time, checking the string in between is dead every time. Repeat on the fifth and third. Then take a melody you know and play it entirely in octaves. Finish by learning the "Third Stone from the Sun" theme.
steps.successCriteria: You can move an octave shape along two string pairs with the middle string silent throughout, play a familiar melody entirely in octaves without a dead note, and play the "Third Stone from the Sun" theme in time.

lessons.title: Jimi Hendrix Third Stone From the Sun Guitar Lesson Bite Sized Blues

steps.title: Pentatonic: minor and major in the same breath
steps.description:
[What it is]
Using the minor pentatonic and the major pentatonic of the same root as one pool: sliding the minor third up to the major third, playing major over the I chord and minor over the IV, and using the blue note between them. In E, the two shapes sit three frets apart and overlap.

[Why it matters]
This is the core of blues-rock lead playing and the sound of his solos over dominant chords, where both thirds are available at once — the same ambiguity that the 7#9 chord contains. A player stuck in the minor box sounds like one mood; a player who can move between the two sounds like the record. The dominant harmony from phase three is what makes it work.

[How to practice]
Play the E minor pentatonic at the twelfth fret and the E major pentatonic at the ninth, then the overlap. Use Pentatonic Best Of play-alongs over blues tracks. Over a 12-bar in E, play one chorus minor only, one major only, then one mixing them with the minor-third-to-major-third slide in every phrase. Listen for where the major sounds right and where it sounds soft.
steps.successCriteria: Over a 12-bar in E you can play a chorus in minor pentatonic, a chorus in major pentatonic, and a chorus mixing them with a minor-to-major third slide in every phrase, without a note that sounds wrong against the chord underneath.

lessons.title: Blend the major and minor pentatonic scales in 1 position - Guitar Lesson - ML074
How to use the Major Pentatonic in a Blues (and sound good)
The Blues Scale (Minor Pentatonic) and the Major Pentatonic Scales on the Guitar

steps.title: Phrasing: space, call and response, and the vocal line
steps.description:
[What it is]
Shaping lines like sung phrases: a short statement, a gap the length of a breath, then an answer that repeats or replies. Notes chosen for where they land rather than for how many there are, with bends and vibrato doing the expressive work.

[Why it matters]
Hendrix came from accompanying singers, and his lead lines are shaped like vocals: they breathe, they repeat, they answer themselves. Guitar Player describes his melodic figures as vocalised. Without phrasing, the vocabulary of the last five steps is just material; with it, the same notes become a solo. This is also the step that keeps the effects in the next phase from becoming the whole personality.

[How to practice]
Play Phrasing — Call & Response over a 12-bar, making every four bars a question and an answer. Then sing a phrase and play it back, keeping the same rhythm and contour. Then record a chorus in which at least half the time is silence, and listen for whether the gaps feel like breathing or like hesitation. Finally take one four-note motif and make a whole chorus from variations of it.
steps.successCriteria: In a recorded chorus over a 12-bar, at least half the time is silence, every four-bar unit is a call and an answer, you can sing any phrase you just played, and one chorus is built entirely from variations of a single four-note motif.

lessons.title: Blues Guitar Lesson (Phrasing) - How To Stop Playing The Pentatonic Scale Up And Down

steps.title: The rig: a flipped Strat into a Marshall
steps.description:
[What it is]
What he actually played and how to get near it. A right-handed Fender Stratocaster restrung and played upside down, mostly mid-sixties models, the best known being the 1968 Olympic White one he played at Woodstock. Into a Marshall Super 100, a JTM45/100 with four-by-twelve cabinets, from 1966 onwards, with the amp loud and the guitar's own controls doing the fine work.

[Why it matters]
Playing a right-handed guitar upside down is not a detail: the controls sit above the strings under his hand, which is why the volume and tone knobs are part of his playing rather than a setup he made once, and the bridge is angled the other way, which changes the string lengths and the bends. And the loud clean-ish Marshall is the reason the fuzz in the next step behaves: a fuzz into a quiet clean amp does not sound like this.

[How to practice]
Play Tone — Match the Reference to build the comparison habit. Then set a crunchy but not saturated amp tone at the loudest volume you can use, so the amp itself is just breaking up. Roll the guitar volume back to 6 and check the tone cleans up; that relationship is the rig. Set the tone control on the bridge pickup rolled slightly back. Record the "Purple Haze" riff and compare with the record, adjusting one control at a time, and write the settings down in words.
steps.successCriteria: You have a saved amp setting that just breaks up at playing volume and cleans up when the guitar volume drops to 6, and a recording of the "Purple Haze" riff on it that sits recognisably close to the record.

lessons.title: Jimi Hendrix - Amp setting revealed, finally! Detailed playthrough and info!

steps.title: Fuzz, and the volume knob as the gain control
steps.description:
[What it is]
A Fuzz Face-style pedal, which he used from 1966 onwards, set flat out in front of a loud amp, and then controlled almost entirely from the guitar: rolled back to about 6 or 7 it cleans up into a thin, glassy rhythm sound, and full up it is the lead tone. Touch does the rest: pick harder and the fuzz responds.

[Why it matters]
This is the single biggest practical difference between his sound and a modern high-gain rig. The pedal is not switched on and off for solos; it stays on and the guitar's volume knob is the control, which is why the same song moves between clean and roaring without a pedal ever moving. It is also why the volume knob's position under his hand, from playing upside down, matters.

[How to practice]
Play Dynamics — Soft to Loud to get the picking-hand control first. Then set a fuzz or fuzz simulation to full in front of the amp tone from the previous step, and practise moving the guitar volume from 10 to 6 to 3 while playing one riff, listening to how the character changes rather than only the loudness. Then play a phrase at three picking intensities without touching any control. Record a part that goes from clean rhythm to fuzz lead using only the knob.
steps.successCriteria: With the fuzz always on you can move from a clean rhythm sound to a full lead sound using only the guitar's volume knob, mid-phrase, and a recording shows three clearly different tones produced by picking intensity alone.

lessons.title: How to get the Hendrix sound using a Fuzz Face

Easy! Jimi Hendrix's Fuzz Tone on any Amp!
Guitar Dynamics Practice: Control Your Tone with This Simple Exercise

steps.title: Wah: as a rhythm instrument and as a voice
steps.description:
[What it is]
The Vox wah used two ways: rocked in time with the strumming hand so the sweep becomes part of the rhythm, as in the "Voodoo Child (Slight Return)" intro, and parked or moved slowly under a lead line so single notes take on a vowel. The pedal sits first in the chain, before the fuzz.

[Why it matters]
The wah is the most recognisable thing about several of his records, and it is almost always played rhythmically rather than waggled. Treated as an instrument it has to be practised like one: the foot is a third limb that has to stay in time. Its position before the fuzz also matters, because that ordering is what produces the vocal quality rather than a thin sweep.

[How to practice]
Set the wah first, before the fuzz. With a metronome at 80 BPM, rock the pedal on the beat with no guitar at all until the motion is steady. Then add muted sixteenth strums and move the pedal on the beat. Then the "Voodoo Child" intro figure with the pedal, from the EricBlackmon lesson. Then Improv — One String over a backing track, moving the pedal slowly to shape single notes rather than to sweep.
steps.successCriteria: With a click at 80 BPM your wah sweep lands on the beat for sixteen bars with muted strums, you can play the "Voodoo Child (Slight Return)" intro figure with the pedal in time, and you can shape a slow single-note line with the pedal without it sounding like a sweep effect.

VOODOO CHILD Jimi Hendrix Guitar Tutorial #6 Wah Part 1 Scratch Guitar Lesson

steps.title: Uni-Vibe, Octavia and the studio tricks
steps.description:
[What it is]
The rest of the sound: a Uni-Vibe, which he used more from 1969, for the swirling pitch-and-phase movement heard on the Woodstock material; the Octavia, built for him by Roger Mayer, which adds a note an octave above and turns single notes into a synthetic squeal; and the studio devices, most famously reversed tape, that made records rather than performances.

[Why it matters]
Wikipedia credits him as one of the first guitarists to make extensive use of tone-altering effects, and as pioneering the guitar as an electronic sound source. Knowing what each device does stops you buying the wrong one and lets you approximate them: a rotary or phaser simulation covers the Uni-Vibe, an octave-fuzz covers the Octavia, and a reversed audio clip covers the tape trick.

[How to practice]
Take one sustained note and play it through, in turn, a phaser or rotary setting, an octave fuzz if you have one, and nothing at all, recording all three. Decide which song section each would belong in. Then record a short phrase, reverse it in any audio editor, and listen to what the attack does; play something designed to be heard backwards. Finally set the Uni-Vibe-style effect slow and shallow under a chord part rather than over a lead, which is how it usually sits.
steps.successCriteria: You have a recording of one sustained note through three treatments (rotary or phaser, octave fuzz or its nearest substitute, and dry) where each is clearly a different part, plus one reversed phrase, and you can say which song section each belongs to.

steps.title: Feedback as an instrument
steps.description:
[What it is]
Standing where the guitar and the amp reinforce each other so a held note blooms into a harmonic instead of decaying, choosing which harmonic by moving, and killing it exactly when the part needs silence. The other half is muting, so only the intended string is free to sing.

[Why it matters]
Feedback in his playing is composed, not accidental: it starts and stops on cue and it is often the loudest melodic event in a song. Wikipedia describes him pioneering the instrument as an electronic sound source, and controlled feedback is the clearest example. It also completes the previous steps, because it only works with the amp loud and the fuzz on.

[How to practice]
Play Muting — One Note at a Time first: feedback control is mostly muting control. Then, at a loud but safe volume, hold a note at the twelfth fret and move slowly towards the speaker until it blooms; mark where you stood. Practise starting the bloom on a chosen beat and stopping it on another. Change the harmonic by moving closer or turning. If you cannot play loud, use a sustain-heavy plugin to practise the timing half.
steps.successCriteria: You can make a fretted note bloom into feedback within two seconds from a repeatable position, start and stop it on chosen beats, change which harmonic sounds by moving, and in a recording nothing but the target note is audible before the bloom.

lessons.title: Guitar Feedback: How to Do It / How to Use It

steps.title: Hey Joe: the R&B chord part
steps.description:
[What it is]
His first single, and the clearest case of the R&B guitarist at work: a descending progression, chords played as partials with the thumb on the bass, fills placed only in the gaps between vocal lines, and a solo that stays close to the chords.

[Why it matters]
MusicRadar lists it among the clean rhythm songs where his touch is most audible, alongside "Bold As Love", "Little Wing" and "Castles Made Of Sand". It is the right first song here because it uses phase one and almost nothing else: if the thumb chords, the partials and the muting are solid, the song plays itself; if not, this is where you find out.

[How to practice]
Learn the progression first as thumb chords, not as barres, using the GuitarLessons365 lesson. Play the whole song comping only, with no fills at all, along with the record, so the placement is right. Then add the fills, using only the gaps. Then learn the solo. Record one take from start to finish and check nothing you play collides with the vocal.
steps.successCriteria: You can play "Hey Joe" with the record from start to finish in the correct tuning, with thumb-fretted partial chords, fills only in the vocal gaps, and the solo in time, in one take without stopping.

steps.title: Purple Haze and Foxey Lady: the fuzz riffs
steps.description:
[What it is]
Two riffs built from chord shapes rather than scales. "Purple Haze" opens on the tritone figure, then the E7#9 with G and A around it. "Foxey Lady" is a single sustained note that blooms into feedback and then a riff drawn from the chord under the fingers, with the sound wide open.

[Why it matters]
These are the songs where the Hendrix chord, the chord riff and the fuzz tone appear together, which is why they come after phases three and five rather than before. They are also a test of restraint: both riffs are simple, and almost everything about how they sound is attack, muting and tone rather than notes.

[How to practice]
"Purple Haze" first: the intro figure, then the riff with the 7#9, then the verse, from the Marty Music lesson. Play with the record at full speed, in the right tuning. Then "Foxey Lady": start with the feedback note from the previous phase, held until it blooms, then the riff. Record both and compare the attack with the records rather than only the notes.
steps.successCriteria: You can play the intro, riff and verse of "Purple Haze" with the record, and the "Foxey Lady" opening including a bloomed feedback note into the riff, both in the correct tuning and with the attack matching the records.

steps.title: Little Wing: the embellishment masterclass
steps.description:
[What it is]
The song that put phase two on record. In E minor, the intro is a series of chords decorated with hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides drawn partly from the key and partly from each chord as it passes: a C sharp appears in the B minor bar, an F natural in the second A minor bar. Every chord is held with the thumb so the fingers can move.

[Why it matters]
It is the single most studied example of his rhythm style, and it is the exam for the embellishment phase: the technique, the note choices and the thumb grip all have to be in place at once. It also shows why the note-choice step mattered, because the fills that sound most like him are exactly the ones that step outside the key.

[How to practice]
Learn it chord by chord, not phrase by phrase: take the first chord and its decorations until they are automatic, then add the next. Use the Garret's Guitar Lessons intro tutorial for the shapes and the Dan Guitar embellishment lesson for the ornaments. Mark on paper which fills are diatonic and which come from the chord. Play with the record at half speed, then full speed.
steps.successCriteria: You can play the "Little Wing" intro with the record at full speed with every chord held by the thumb and the decorations ringing over it, and you can point to the two fills that come from outside the key and name their notes.

Little Wing Beginner Guitar Lesson #2 - Hendrix Embellishments

steps.title: The Wind Cries Mary and Castles Made of Sand
steps.description:
[What it is]
Two ballads from the same vocabulary as "Little Wing" but with different problems. "The Wind Cries Mary" has a bass line walking under the chords and fills that answer the vocal line directly. "Castles Made of Sand" adds slides between voicings and a solo that is as much texture as melody.

[Why it matters]
Between them they cover the two remaining steps of phase two, the moving bass and the sliding voicings, in a real setting. They are also where the R&B accompaniment discipline pays off most audibly: both songs are built around a vocal, and the guitar's job is to fill the gaps and then get out of the way.

[How to practice]
"The Wind Cries Mary" first, from the Jon MacLennan or Tim Pierce lesson, learning the intro bass movement before the chords. Play it with the record and mark every place where you cover the vocal; remove those notes. Then "Castles Made of Sand", with the slides learned as deliberate arrivals. Record both and listen for the space.
steps.successCriteria: You can play both songs with the records in the correct tuning without stopping, with the bass movement audible under "The Wind Cries Mary", the slides in "Castles Made of Sand" landing on the beat, and no fill covering a vocal line.

steps.title: Red House: the slow blues
steps.description:
[What it is]
His blues showpiece: a 12-bar in a triplet feel, an unaccompanied intro that states the whole vocabulary in twelve bars, and choruses that build from sparse phrases to dense ones. Everything from the lead phase appears here, and nothing else has to.

[Why it matters]
This is where the roadmap's two halves meet: the blues rooted in Muddy Waters, B.B. King and Howlin' Wolf, played with his bends, vibrato and double stops, over the shuffle feel from phase three. It is also the most exposed setting for the bending work, because a slow blues gives every note time to be out of tune.

[How to practice]
Learn the intro from the GuitarForce or Pow Music breakdown, bar by bar, checking every bend against a reference. Then play the 12-bar comping only, with thumb chords in a triplet feel. Then improvise a chorus using the phrasing rules from phase four: half silence, calls and answers. Record three choruses that build in density and check the last one has not become busy for its own sake.
steps.successCriteria: You can play the "Red House" intro with every bend in tune against the record, comp a 12-bar in a triplet feel with thumb chords, and improvise three choruses that build in density, with at least half of the first chorus being silence.

steps.title: Voodoo Child (Slight Return)
steps.description:
[What it is]
The song that needs everything at once: the wah-driven opening played rhythmically rather than swept, the main riff built from a chord shape with the wah still moving, a comping part behind the vocal, and a solo that uses bends, double stops and the whole neck.

[Why it matters]
It is the summary piece of the whole roadmap. The intro alone requires the wah technique, the muting and the chord-riff approach simultaneously, and the solo requires the lead phase. It is also the piece where being in the right tuning and having the right relationship between fuzz and volume knob is most obvious.

[How to practice]
The intro first, with the wah, at half speed with a metronome so the pedal lands on the beat, using the EricBlackmon wah breakdown alongside a tab lesson. Then the main riff and the verse comping. Then the solo in sections from the Marty Music or Mr. Tabs lesson. Play the whole song with the record, then with a drum track only.
steps.successCriteria: You can play the intro, riff, verse comping and solo of "Voodoo Child (Slight Return)" with the record without stopping, with the wah landing on the beat throughout and the tuning and fuzz-to-volume relationship matching the earlier phases.

Jimi Hendrix - Voodoo Child (Slight Return) - Guitar Tab | Lesson | Cover | Tutorial

VOODOO CHILD Jimi Hendrix Guitar Tutorial #6 Wah Part 1 Scratch Guitar Lesson

steps.title: All Along the Watchtower: four solos, one arrangement
steps.description:
[What it is]
A cover turned into an arrangement: a chord part that carries the whole song, then a sequence of solo sections, each with its own character, including a slide passage and a wah-and-fuzz section. From Electric Ladyland (1968).

[Why it matters]
It is the clearest demonstration of arrangement thinking in his catalogue: the solos are not one long improvisation but a series of designed statements, each with a different sound and a different idea. Learning it teaches you to plan a solo section rather than fill it, which is what the final phase asks for.

[How to practice]
Learn the rhythm part first and play the whole song with it alone. Then take the solo sections one at a time from the Marty Music series, and for each write down in one sentence what its idea is before you play it. Play the whole song with the record. Then play it again improvising your own material in one of the solo slots, keeping that slot's character.
steps.successCriteria: You can play "All Along the Watchtower" with the record from start to finish including the solo sections, describe each solo section's idea in a sentence, and improvise your own material in one of the slots while keeping that section's character.

lessons.title: Jimi Hendrix All Along The Watchtower Guitar Lesson + Tutorial (Part 1)
Jimi Hendrix All Along The Watchtower Guitar Lesson + Tutorial (Part 2) - The First Solo Interlude
JIMI HENDRIX All Along The Watchtower GUITAR LESSON Solos

steps.title: Improvising in the style
steps.description:
[What it is]
Improvising over a dominant vamp or a 12-bar with his vocabulary and nobody else's: mixed pentatonics, double stops, octaves, bends that resolve, space between phrases, and a return to the rhythm part when the idea runs out.

[Why it matters]
Learning his songs proves you can copy; this proves you can speak. It is also where the constraint matters most, because the easy failure is to play modern blues-rock with a fuzz pedal on. A checklist of his devices keeps the improvisation honest without making it mechanical.

[How to practice]
Play Improv Prompts — Medium so you are used to improvising under a constraint. Then over an E7 vamp record three choruses and check them against a list: a mixed major and minor phrase, a double stop, an octave figure, a bend that resolves, at least half the time silent, and one return to the chord part. Re-record until at least five of the six appear without being forced.
steps.successCriteria: You have a recorded three-chorus improvisation over an E7 vamp in which a listener with the six-item checklist can tick at least five, and you can say where each happens.

lessons.title: Blues Guitar Lesson (Phrasing) - How To Stop Playing The Pentatonic Scale Up And Down

steps.title: Rhythm and lead as one part
steps.description:
[What it is]
Playing a part that is both at once: the chord part continues while fills and lead phrases come out of it and return to it, with no gap where the rhythm drops out. The thumb keeps the bass, the fingers move, and the lead is made from the same shapes.

[Why it matters]
In a trio there is no second guitar, so when the guitarist solos the harmony disappears unless the part is built this way. It is the reason his live recordings sound full with three people on stage. This step is also the true integration of phases one, two and four: the embellishment method extended until the decorations become the solo.

[How to practice]
Play Improv — One Chord over a static backing so there is nothing to hide behind. Then play a two-chord vamp and give yourself one rule: never stop the chord part for more than two beats. Every lead idea must start from a chord tone under your fingers and end back on the chord. Record two minutes and listen for the moment the harmony disappears; fix that moment.
steps.successCriteria: In a two-minute recording over a two-chord vamp the chord part never stops for more than two beats, every lead phrase starts from a chord tone and returns to the chord, and a listener can still hear the harmony throughout.

lessons.title: Embellish Your Rhythms + Chords Like Hendrix

steps.title: Playing in a trio
steps.description:
[What it is]
Playing with bass and drums and nothing else: holding the arrangement alone, cueing section changes with dynamics rather than words, dropping to almost nothing behind a vocal, and recovering from a mistake without stopping. With musicians or with a bass-and-drums play-along.

[Why it matters]
The Experience was a trio, and everything in this roadmap was designed for that format: the thumb bass, the partial chords, the rhythm-and-lead part and the loud amp all exist because there is nobody else. Playing it with a rhythm section is where you find out whether the part is actually self-sufficient.

[How to practice]
Play Timing — Switch Subdivisions to keep the pocket while the density changes. Then play a 12-bar in E with other players or a play-along: two choruses comping, two soloing, back to comping, signalling each change with a dynamic move rather than a count. Make one deliberate mistake per run and carry on. Record five minutes and check the bass and drums are still audible under you.
steps.successCriteria: A five-minute trio or play-along recording of a 12-bar in E has clear comp and solo sections signalled by dynamics, the bass and drums audible throughout, and one deliberate mistake you recover from without stopping.

lessons.title: Guitar lessons: Soloing in a trio

steps.title: Final: a recorded Hendrix set
steps.description:
[What it is]
Three pieces recorded back to back in one sitting: one R&B or ballad song where the rhythm playing carries it, one fuzz-driven riff song, and one blues or extended song with your own solo in it. In the right tuning, on your version of his sound, with the tone changes worked out in advance.

[Why it matters]
It is the roadmap's promise made checkable, and it covers the three sides of him that the phases were built around: the accompanist, the riff writer and the improviser. Recording is also the only honest judge of the things that matter most here — whether the bends are in tune, whether the muting is clean, and whether there is any space.

[How to practice]
Choose the three songs and write a one-page plan: tuning check, tone setting per song, where your own solo goes, how each starts and ends. Rehearse the transitions, not just the songs. Record the set in one sitting, listen once for tuning, once for timing, once for space, and re-record the weakest of the three.

[What you can do now]
You play his rhythm style with thumb chords, partials, sliding sixths and muted comping; you decorate chords the way "Little Wing" does and can choose the notes deliberately; you use 7#9 and dominant voicings to build chord riffs; you bend in tune, use hand and bar vibrato, double stops and octaves, and mix major and minor pentatonic; you can set up a Strat-and-fuzz sound and control it from the guitar; you can play seven of his songs; and you can improvise and carry a trio in his language.
steps.successCriteria: You have three recordings made in one sitting — an R&B or ballad song, a fuzz riff song, and a blues or extended song containing your own solo — all in the correct tuning, each played through without stopping, with the tone changed deliberately between them.
